agenda.say: Good morning, and welcome to Case Management. Before a single lesson, a quick game: two truths and a lie, Case Manager edition. I say three things about the job, you vote with your hands. One: a Case Manager can tell a client what their case is worth. Two: if it isn't in the CMS, it didn't happen. Three: the Conflict Check comes before the matter is even opened. {name}, which one's the lie? Number one, and by lunch you'll know exactly why. Here's how today runs. First the lessons: your role, John Doe's case, the line between sharing facts and giving legal advice, reading the raw file, the Case Plan and his treatment, then the car side of things, the do's and don'ts, the repair, the rental. Then the Practice Lab, four Skill Activities on his real file. Then the Knowledge Check. By the end of today his matter is open the right way, and his car problem has a plan. Now the teaser. Somewhere on John Doe's file there's a damaged car, and nobody has worked out yet whose it is. That one detail decides who gets a rental. I'm keeping the answer until this afternoon. And a confession: my first week, I thought CMS stood for Can't Miss Saturday. It doesn't, but you'll still never miss a deadline in it.
agenda.ask: {name}, of everything on today's agenda, which part do you think a brand-new Case Manager gets wrong most often?

lab.say: Quick show of hands: who has ever built flat-pack furniture without reading the instructions? Keep your hand up if there were screws left over. {name}, I see you, and I respect the honesty. This is the Practice Lab, and today there are no leftover screws. Open the tools on this slide now, the CMS first, and keep it open beside the slides. We run four Skill Activities on John Doe's real file, in order. First, open his case in the CMS, with the Conflict Check before anything else. Second, build his onboarding Direction Packet, his do's and don'ts. Third, assign those directions in the system. Fourth, the Civic investigation: whose rental is it, really? Each one runs the same way: Your Case, Your Task, then Check Your Work. The lazy version is clicking until the screen turns green. The high-value version is every field matching a document, every correction with its source, every step logged. Why so fussy? Months from now an adjuster reads this file, and what you type today is page one of the story they believe. {name}, you're my CMS navigator. {name}, you're my fact checker. Stuck on one step for more than ten minutes? Log what you have and move on; we fix it in the debrief. And a mystery: a helpful colleague has already left a mistake waiting for you in activity one.
lab.ask: {name}, before you click anything, which document will you keep open beside the CMS, and why that one?

wrap.say: Before the Knowledge Check, let's step back. Quick game first: finish this sentence, one breath each. On a brand-new file, the one thing I will never do is… {name}, go. {name}, you're next. Love it. Now the real question for the room. Robert Smith's insurance company has already called John Doe, and he needs a car to get to work. What do you tell him today, in what order, and what has to be on the file before tomorrow's claim set-up? Here's the lazy answer: don't talk to them, we'll handle it, bye. Here's the high-value one: the do's and don'ts in plain words, the rental path laid out, every step logged the same day, and anything legal routed to Atty. Thorne. I once had a client who, trying to be helpful, told the other side's adjuster his whole life story, including the part about his old football knee. That knee showed up in every offer for a year. What John says this week lives in the adjuster's notes for the life of the case. So take two or three answers, and tie each one to a moment on his file from today. Then your mystery for tonight: tomorrow we send the letters that tell every insurance company we represent him. How many companies is that, and which one would John never have guessed is involved?
wrap.ask: {name}, what's the very first thing you'd tell John Doe, and why that first?
